meta.title: Automated Satellite Conjunction Management with Transformer-Based Bayesian Deep Learning Approach
meta.authorsHtml: Amirah Almutairi<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Jana Redaini<sup>1</sup>, Rana Alzahrani<sup>1</sup>, Mai Fadel<sup>1</sup>

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: The rapid growth of satellite mega-constellations in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) has increased the frequency of conjunction events, creating a need for reliable collision-risk assessment tools. Conjunction Data Messages (CDMs) provide sequential updates during close approaches, but their analysis is challenging due to orbital uncertainty and the increasing volume of conjunction data. This paper proposes an uncertainty-aware framework for Next-CDM prediction using a Transformer Encoder (TE) architecture. The TE leverages self-attention to capture temporal dependencies across CDM sequences and is evaluated as an alternative to recurrent architectures for modeling successive conjunction updates. The framework integrates Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout for epistemic uncertainty estimation and conformal calibration to improve the reliability of predictive intervals. The framework is evaluated against LSTM, GRU, and Last-CDM baselines using the ESA Kelvins dataset and the Aldoria dataset. The TE achieved the lowest deterministic mean squared error (MSE) on both datasets, with values of 0.1566 on Kelvins and 0.1061 on Aldoria, while also attaining the strongest uncertainty ranking and requiring fewer trainable parameters than the recurrent baselines. Computationally, the TE achieved faster inference on the larger Kelvins workload. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of the TE for accurate and uncertainty-aware Next-CDM prediction.

blocks.html: The rapid growth of satellite deployments in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) has increased orbital congestion. Debris from expired satellites, fragmentation events, and launch-related remnants continues to accumulate [1]. This problem has intensified with the expansion of commercial megaconstellations such as Starlink, which increase the frequency of close approaches between operational spacecraft and debris [2]. Such congestion also raises the risk of cascading collision events known as the Kessler syndrome, where collisions generate additional debris and increase the probability of future impacts [3].

Monitoring and mitigation rely on orbital tracking networks that detect potential conjunctions and issue Conjunction Data Messages (CDMs) [4]. A CDM is a standardized report containing orbital vectors, covariance estimates, and collision-related information. During a conjunction event, CDMs are issued sequentially until the Time of Closest Approach (TCA), providing an evolving representation of the conjunction [5]. However, analyzing these sequential updates depends largely on manual interpretation, limiting scalability in increasingly dense orbital environments [5, 6].

Machine learning methods have been explored for automated conjunction assessment. Early approaches focused on predicting risk levels or classifying conjunction events [7, 8], while subsequent work modeled CDM sequence evolution directly. Pinto et al. [9] introduced a Bayesian LSTM-based approach for Next-CDM prediction and applied Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout to estimate predictive uncertainty. Other gated recurrent architectures, such as GRU, provide a simpler recurrent alternative for modeling sequential data [10]. While recurrent architectures are well suited to sequential data, they process observations sequentially, whereas Transformer architectures use self-attention to capture dependencies across sequence positions [11].

In this work, we investigate a Transformer Encoder (TE) architecture for Next-CDM prediction, following the encoder-based approach of Jeong and Shin [12], who demonstrated its potential for accurate and computationally efficient orbit prediction. While their work focuses on periodic orbital data derived from two-line elements (TLEs), CDMs are issued as irregular, event-driven updates. Accordingly, the TE is adapted to model CDM sequences and predict the next recorded CDM from the preceding history. MC Dropout is used to estimate predictive uncertainty, followed by conformal calibration to improve prediction-interval reliability. The TE is evaluated against LSTM, GRU, and a deterministic Last-CDM baseline under the same data partitions and experimental procedure.

To evaluate Next-CDM prediction across different sequence characteristics, this study uses two CDM datasets. The first dataset was provided by Aldoria through the DebriSolver Challenge organized by the Saudi Space Agency [13]. It contains orbital state vectors for both objects, covariance information, and conjunction-related parameters.

The second is the ESA Kelvins 2021 Collision Avoidance Challenge dataset [14], which contains CDM sequences associated with conjunction events and provides longer event histories. Dataset-specific preprocessing, filtering, and feature selection were applied before sequence construction, as described in the Data Preprocessing subsection.

Several preprocessing steps were applied to clean and standardize the Aldoria dataset. Non-informative variables and all columns containing more than 50% missing values were removed to exclude features with insufficient information. Events were then filtered to retain only those containing three or more CDM messages, ensuring sufficient temporal information for predicting the next CDM in a sequence. Covariance parameters were converted to numerical form, and outliers were clipped within the 0.1%-99.9% percentile range to reduce the effect of extreme values. Messages within each event were chronologically ordered using creation_date, and the final feature set included key orbital variables, cross-sectional area characteristics, and covariance matrix elements.

After preprocessing, the Aldoria dataset contained 10,593 rows from 3,082 events and 29 features. All numerical features were standardized using the z-score method to address differences in value ranges. The Kelvins dataset was processed using the preprocessing pipeline and filtering criteria described in Pinto et al. [9], resulting in 136,481 rows from 9,835 events and 60 features.

CDMs belonging to the same conjunction event form an ordered multivariate sequence, with each message providing an updated description of the evolving event. This structure enables self-attention to capture dependencies across the observed CDM history. Since the task is formulated as Next-CDM regression rather than mapping between separate source and target sequences, only the encoder component of the Transformer is used. This avoids introducing a decoder and cross-attention mechanism while retaining the ability to model temporal dependencies across the sequence.

As illustrated in Figure 1, the TE is trained on timeshifted CDM sequences. For an event containing T CDM messages, the input sequence spans CDM(0) to CDM(T − 2), while the corresponding target sequence spans CDM(1) to CDM(T −1). During inference, the observed CDM history is provided to the model, and the output at the final valid position is used to predict the next CDM.

The predictive model is based on a TE architecture, as shown in Figure 2. The input CDM features are first mapped to a dmodel-dimensional latent representation through a linear projection, followed by fixed sinusoidal positional encoding. The resulting sequence is processed by two Transformer encoder layers with four-head selfattention.

Quantifying predictive uncertainty is particularly important in satellite conjunction management, where point predictions alone do not indicate the reliability of the predicted conjunction evolution. To complement the Next-CDM predictions, MC Dropout is used to estimate epistemic uncertainty by retaining dropout during inference and performing T stochastic forward passes [15]. Raw prediction intervals are constructed from empirical MC quantiles. Conformal calibration is then applied using a separate event-disjoint calibration partition to improve coverage [17]. Calibration is performed independently for each feature and coverage level without modifying the predictive mean or standard deviation.

Simultaneous conformal calibration is additionally applied to three operational quantities: time-to-TCA, miss distance, and relative speed for ESA Kelvins, and TCA, miss distance, and relative speed for Aldoria. An event is jointly covered only when all three quantities fall within their calibrated intervals [18].

For the experiments, both datasets were partitioned at the event level into training, checkpoint-validation, calibration, and test sets. The ESA Kelvins dataset was divided using ratios of 68%, 8.5%, 8.5%, and 15%, respectively, while the Aldoria dataset used 64%, 8%, 8%, and 20%, with a fixed random seed of 42. The TE was compared with LSTM [19], GRU [10], and Last-CDM, a persistence baseline defined as ˆxt+1 = xt. The LSTM baseline and Next-CDM prediction formulation were based on Pinto et al. [9], and all models within each dataset used the same partitions and evaluation protocol.

All trainable models used Adam with a learning rate of 10−4, a batch size of 128, a maximum of 500 epochs, early-stopping patience of 50, and gradient clipping with a maximum norm of 1.0. The model state with the lowest checkpoint-validation masked MSE was restored for evaluation. The TE used dmodel = 128, two encoder layers, four attention heads, a feed-forward dimension of 512, GELU activation, and a dropout probability of 0.2.

Prediction performance was evaluated using deterministic standardized MSE over valid Next-CDM transitions, excluding padded positions and originally missing targets. Computational efficiency was assessed using the number of trainable parameters and deterministic inference time measured over the complete test set under a consistent timing protocol across models.

MC Dropout was evaluated using 1, 50, and 200 stochastic forward passes, with 200 passes used for the final uncertainty and calibration analyses. Evaluation was performed at the final valid Next-CDM prediction of each event, with empirical coverage assessed at 50%, 80%, 90%, and 95%. Uncertainty ranking was evaluated using Spearman correlation and partial AURC over coverage levels from 0.10 to 1.00, while feature-wise and simultaneous conformal calibration used the separate calibration partitions.

The prediction performance of the TE model was compared with LSTM, GRU, and Last-CDM using the deterministic standardized MSE over all valid Next-CDM transitions. The results for both datasets are presented in Table 1.

The TE achieved the lowest MSE on both datasets. For the ESA Kelvins dataset, the TE reduced the MSE by approximately 14.5% compared with LSTM, 12.7% compared with GRU, and 27.5% compared with Last-CDM. For the Aldoria dataset, the corresponding reductions were approximately 10.8%, 11.5%, and 33.1%, respectively.

blocks.html: The per-feature analysis further demonstrated that the performance gains of the TE were distributed consistently across the predicted variables rather than concentrated in a limited subset. On ESA Kelvins, the TE achieved lower MSE than LSTM for 59 of 60 features and than GRU for all 60 features. On Aldoria, it achieved lower MSE than LSTM for all 29 features and than GRU for 28 of 29 features. These findings indicate that the TE provided a consistent performance advantage over the recurrent baselines across the modeled CDM variables.

blocks.html: Among the trainable models, the TE had the fewest parameters on both datasets, indicating a more compact model configuration. Compared with LSTM and GRU, it used 52.5% and 37.0% fewer parameters on ESA Kelvins, and 51.2% and 35.1% fewer on Aldoria, respectively. However, inference-time performance differed between the datasets. On ESA Kelvins, the TE achieved the lowest mean inference time at 19.713 ms, whereas on Aldoria, GRU was fastest at 7.271 ms, followed closely by LSTM.

Although the TE consistently required fewer parameters, its inference-time advantage varied with sequence length. To examine this behavior, an additional experiment was conducted on ESA Kelvins using maximum sequence lengths of three and four CDMs. GRU achieved lower inference latency in both settings, suggesting that the computational advantage of the TE becomes more apparent for longer sequences, whereas recurrent models may be more efficient for shorter sequences. This relationship, however, may also depend on the hardware and implementation settings.

blocks.html: A single stochastic forward pass produced higher MSE than deterministic inference for all trainable models on both datasets. Averaging multiple stochastic predictions reduced this difference, with MC50 and MC200 approaching deterministic performance. The small difference between MC50 and MC200 suggests increasing stability of the predictive mean as the number of stochastic samples increases. The TE consistently achieved the lowest MSE across all MC settings, preserving the deterministic ranking.
However, MC200 did not outperform deterministic inference, indicating that MC Dropout primarily supports uncertainty estimation rather than improving point-prediction accuracy.

Predictive-interval reliability was assessed by comparing empirical and nominal coverage. On ESA Kelvins, the raw MC Dropout intervals were generally conservative across the operational features, resulting in relatively small calibration changes for time-to-TCA, miss distance, and relative speed.

On Aldoria, the raw uncertainty estimates varied substantially across the operational features. Miss distance showed pronounced undercoverage, whereas TCA and relative speed showed substantial overcoverage. At the 90% nominal level, raw miss-distance coverage was 31.77% for TE, 37.93% for LSTM, and 35.66% for GRU. Following conformal calibration, these values increased to 94.00%, 93.52%, and 93.35%, respectively, substantially correcting the undercoverage while the overcovered features remained conservative.

The ability of the estimated uncertainty to distinguish lower- from higher-error events was further evaluated using the Spearman uncertainty–error correlation and partial AURC. The results are summarized in Table 4.

blocks.html: On ESA Kelvins, the TE achieved the strongest uncertainty ranking, with the highest Spearman correlation of 0.421 and the lowest partial AURC of 0.103. This indicates that its estimated uncertainty was more informative for distinguishing higher- from lower-error events than those of the recurrent baselines. On Aldoria, the TE again achieved the highest Spearman correlation of 0.147 and the lowest partial AURC of 0.353. Although uncertainty-ranking performance was weaker on Aldoria than on ESA Kelvins, the TE remained the best-performing model according to both metrics.

Finally, simultaneous conformal calibration was evaluated for the three operational quantities, with an event considered covered only when all three quantities fell within their calibrated intervals. At the 90% nominal level, joint coverage on ESA Kelvins changed from 91.74% to 92.01% for TE, 87.30% to 90.85% for LSTM, and 89.28% to 92.56% for GRU. On Aldoria, the improvement was substantially larger, increasing from 31.77% to 94.00% for TE, 37.60% to 93.52% for LSTM, and 35.01% to 93.35% for GRU. These results show that the simultaneous conformal calibration improved joint coverage reliability, particularly on Aldoria, where the raw intervals provided inadequate simultaneous coverage.

The experimental results show that the TE provides effective predictive modeling of CDM sequences, achieving the lowest MSE on both datasets compared with LSTM, GRU, and Last-CDM baselines. The TE also showed the strongest uncertainty ranking among the evaluated models, particularly on ESA Kelvins. MC Dropout enabled uncertainty estimation without improving point-prediction accuracy, while conformal calibration improved predictive coverage when the raw intervals were insufficient. Together, these results support the use of self-attention with uncertainty estimation and calibration for Next-CDM prediction.

Looking at computational efficiency, the TE required fewer trainable parameters than the recurrent models and achieved faster inference on ESA Kelvins, whereas the recurrent models were faster on Aldoria. The additional sequence-length analysis suggests that sequence length contributes to this difference, with the computational advantage of the TE becoming more apparent for longer sequences, whereas recurrent architectures can be more efficient for very short sequences under the evaluated hardware and implementation settings.

Future work will focus on further evaluating the generalization of the proposed framework across additional CDM datasets and extending the current one-step formulation to longer-horizon prediction. Broader statistical analyses and alternative uncertainty methods could also be investigated to assess prediction reliability. Finally, the framework could be developed into a reusable software library for CDM prediction, uncertainty estimation, and conjunction analysis.
